summary: Children aged 9–10 rank several chance events from least to most likely, including unequal outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections). Same-total comparisons yield to simple more/less reasoning; comparing across different totals demands proportional reasoning, which research shows develops slowly. Teaching should secure confident additive comparison, then nudge attention from absolute counts toward the proportion of favourable outcomes. The signature task sets up a case where the bag with MORE red counters has a LOWER chance of red (3 red of 4 vs 6 red of 12), and uses repeated sampling to let a count-based guess be publicly corrected by a long-run tally.
misconceptions: Comparing by absolute count of favourable outcomes ('Bag B has 6 reds, Bag A only 3, so B is better') instead of proportion
The 'difference' strategy — comparing by the gap between the two colours (reds minus blues) rather than the fraction of the whole
Equiprobability bias — 'it's random, so every bag/colour is equally likely and you can't rank them'
Ranking by personal desire or by which outcome happened last, rather than by composition

activities.title: Rank two bags, then test by sampling
steps: Look at Bag A (3 red, 1 blue) and Bag B (6 red, 6 blue), both fully visible, and rank which gives the better chance of pulling red before any draws.
State a reason for the ranking out loud.

Draw many times from each bag (e.g. 50 draws each), noting each drawn counter's colour and returning it to the bag before the next draw so the proportion stays fixed, and tally how often red comes up, comparing the two tallies.
Revise the ranking if the tally contradicts the first guess, and say why — in terms of how big a share of each bag is red, not how many reds.
Look at a shaded red-fraction strip beside each tally (three-quarters of A, one-half of B) and connect the share to the observed long-run frequency.

As an extension, suppose Bag B instead held 60 red and 40 blue: check whether these bigger numbers change the ranking (60 of 100 is three-fifths, higher than one-half but still below Bag A's three-quarters, so Bag A is still the better bet).
activities.insight: A better chance of red depends on the proportion of red in the whole bag (three-quarters beats one-half), not on the raw number of red counters — so a bag with more reds can still be the worse bet.

activities.title: Order four or more events on a least→most-likely line
steps: Physically place four or more event cards along a 'least likely → most likely' rail (e.g. different bags or spinners with varying red fractions).
Defend each placement, and each time a card is moved, say why it should sit higher or lower.
Respond to a challenge such as 'why is that one higher? what if I doubled the blues?' by giving a reason in terms of the share of the whole, not just the number of reds.
Start with cards that share the same total (so simple more/less reasoning works) before mixing in cards with different totals.
activities.insight: Events can be placed in a consistent order of likelihood by comparing the proportion of favourable outcomes; same-total cases need only more/less, but different-total cases need the share of the whole.

activities.title: Spinner prediction: does section size matter?
steps: Look at a spinner where red fills three-quarters and blue one-quarter, alongside a fair coin.
Before spinning, predict: over 20 spins, will red and blue come up about the same number of times, or will one come up much more — and state a reason.
Spin 20 times and tally red versus blue (expect red near 15, blue near 5).
Compare the tally to the prediction and explain what the size of each section did to the outcome.
Consider follow-ups: could the less-likely colour still come up on the very next spin? What does 'more likely' actually mean here?
activities.insight: When outcomes are not equally sized, 'it could land on either' does not make them equally likely — the size (proportion) of each section governs the long-run frequency, and a more-likely outcome can still fail on a single trial.

activities.title: The 'difference' trap: 20 red vs 18 blue
steps: Compare a bag of 20 red and 18 blue with a clearly lopsided bag of 3 red and 1 blue, and decide which gives the better chance of red. Notice that BOTH bags have the same gap: 2 more reds than blues.
Explain the reasoning, noticing whether it rests on the gap between the colours (reds minus blues) or on the share of the whole.
Work out what share of each bag is red (close to one-half for 20 of 38, three-quarters for 3 of 4) and use that to place both in order.
Check the conclusion by sampling (with each counter returned before the next draw) if a count-based or difference-based answer is given.
activities.insight: Comparing by the gap between the two colours (reds minus blues) can mislead: 20 red and 18 blue and 3 red and 1 blue both have a gap of 2, yet 20 of 38 is almost an even chance while 3 of 4 is three-quarters — so the fraction of the whole, not the surplus of reds, decides likelihood.

checkQuestion: Show two bags of counters, both visible. Bag A: 3 red and 1 blue. Bag B: 6 red and 6 blue. Ask: 'Which bag gives you a better chance of pulling out a red — and why?' Take their answer, then ask them to explain their reason fully (Tier 2).
checkAnswer: Bag A. Even though Bag B contains more red counters (6 versus 3), three of the four counters in Bag A are red — three-quarters — while only six of the twelve in Bag B are red — one half. Bag A has the higher proportion of red, so a better chance.
